newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY FORECASTS ECONOMIC INDICATORS FOR 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY FORECASTS ECONOMIC INDICATORS FOR 1996/97.

text.p: Hungary's inflation will be around 23 percent this year, the current account deficit below $1.5 billion and the gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 0.5 percent, while the volume of investments will be flat, the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday.

Secretary of State Tibor Draskovics told a conference organised by the German-Hungarian Economic Chamber that Hungary has created the conditions of economic growth and will continue its strict budgetary politics in 1997.

"The Hungarian economy can expect modest but well-supported economic growth in 1997," he said, adding that the GDP was likely to grow by two to three percent next year. "We hope that this will be the first year of a long trend," he said.

Hungary has laid down the foundations of a market economy, which in the past two years has stabilised after a slump following the collapse of the communist trading bloc Comecon in the early 1990s, Draskovics said.
The role of the state in the economy, as well as overspending of the government and the population has been radically reduced in the past two years, he said.

As a painful effect of economic austerity, real wages dropped some 15 percent in the past two years, but they are likely to remain unchanged next year and domestic consumption may even show modest growth in 1997, Draskovics said.
As a result of strict economic plicies, inflation was likely to drop to about 23 percent this year -- instead of the 20 percent target -- and to 18 percent next year, he said.
However, the current account deficit will probably be lower than the forecast $2 billion, and will be below $1.5 billion, compared with $2.5 billion in 1995, he added.

Investments, which dropped in the first nine months, will pick up by the end of the year, partly driven by a promising growth rate of around 20 percent in the processing industry, agriculture and housing construction, and a 40 percent increase in machinery industry exports reached this year, he said.
He added the government was determined to further reduce its revenues and expenditures in 1997, begin the reform of the pension system and improve the profitability of entreprises.
The proportion of state redistribution to the GDP will drop to 47-48 percent in 1997 from 60 percent in 1994, while the profits of company profits will increase by three times, Draskovics said.
The pension system's planned reform was seen boosting private pension funds, creating extra development sources of 30 to 40 billion forints for the economy by end-1998, he added.

The main uncertainty factors for Hungary for 1997 were the performance of the economies of its trading partners and the behaviour of the Hungarian-owned companies which failed to increase investments this year due to their concerns over depressed domestic consumption, Draskovics said.
